evidence: More and more, younger people are being diagnosed with type 2 diabetes.
In England, for example, the biggest increase in new diagnoses of type 2 diabetes is among young women.

nary_nodes.label: Misra on focus on ethnic minority groups
evidence: "Much of the discussion around rising type 2 diabetes in younger people has focused on ethnic minority groups," said Shivani Misra, the lead author of the study and a clinical associate professor for diabetes at Imperial College London.

nary_nodes.label: Misra on T2D incidence in white populations
evidence: "While these ethnic groups are disproportionately affected with early-onset type 2 diabetes, we now see that incidence is […] increasing in white populations too, showing that this public health challenge is broadening across the generation."

nary_nodes.label: Gallwitz on Germany's T2D situation
evidence: In Germany, the situation is similar to the UK, said Baptist Gallwitz, an endocrinologist and spokesperson for the German Diabetes Society (DDG).

nary_nodes.label: Gallwitz on T2D as a pandemic
evidence: "Type 2 diabetes is on the rise in many countries," Gallwitz told DW.
"It's basically a pandemic."

nary_nodes.label: T2D cases increase in German youth
evidence: In Germany, we're also seeing an increase in children and teenagers diagnosed with the disease.

nary_nodes.label: DDG report on youth T2D increase
evidence: From 2014 to 2023, there was an increase in type 2 diabetes cases of 5.8% a year among youth aged 11 to 17 years, according to a 2026 health report on diabetes released by the DDG.

nary_nodes.label: Gallwitz on lifestyle factors for T2D
evidence: "We live in a world where we don't move enough and where our nutrition contains too much sugar and too many calories," Gallwitz said.
"That leads to more obesity among young people, and that in turn greatly increases the risk of type 2 diabetes."

nary_nodes.label: T2D mechanism: insulin resistance/deficiency
evidence: In people with type 2 diabetes, reduced insulin secretion or a weaker effect of insulin on its receptors lead to a higher glucose content in the blood.

evidence: Type 1 diabetes is characterized by a full loss of insulin-producing cells, leading to severe insulin deficiency.

evidence: "Any diagnosis of type 2 diabetes is serious, but it can be more aggressive in younger people, increasing the risk of devastating complications and cutting lives short," said Helen Kirrane from Diabetes UK, a charity that campaigns on the issue.

nary_nodes.label: Kautzky-Willer on general environment
evidence: But conditions in the general environment also need to be improved to stop the increase of type 2 diabetes in young women, said Alexandra Kautzky-Willer, head of the division for endocrinology and metabolism at the Medical University of Vienna.

nary_nodes.label: Kautzky-Willer on safe movement conditions
evidence: "More movement is important, so we need to ensure conditions in which it's safe for women to move," Kautzky-Willer, who is also a professor of gender medicine, told DW.

nary_nodes.label: Kautzky-Willer on T2D underdiagnosis in women
evidence: In 2025, Kautzky-Willer and a colleague wrote a report for the Deutsches Ärzteblatt, a German medical journal, saying that the disease is underdiagnosed in women.

nary_nodes.label: Report: Men diagnosed younger with T2D
evidence: "Men are usually diagnosed with [type 2 diabetes] at a younger age," they wrote in the the article.

nary_nodes.label: Report: Women's condition at T2D diagnosis
evidence: "At the point of diagnosis, more women are obese, they have hypertension more often and have gained more weight" than men when they are diagnosed.

nary_nodes.label: Kautzky-Willer on fasting blood sugar test
evidence: "For one, the value often tested in initial diabetes diagnosis is fasting blood sugar," Kautzky-Willer said.

nary_nodes.label: Kautzky-Willer on fasting blood sugar in women
evidence: Fasting blood sugar "is generally lower in women than it is in men," Kautzky-Willer said.

nary_nodes.label: Kautzky-Willer on glucose tolerance test
evidence: "It would make more sense to do a glucose tolerance test, but that is more work."

nary_nodes.label: Kautzky-Willer on HbA1c levels test
evidence: Kautzky-Willer says it would be good if HbA1c levels were tested as well.

nary_nodes.label: Glycated haemoglobin formation
evidence: HbA1c refers to glycated haemoglobin, which is when glucose in your body sticks to red blood cells.

evidence: A high HbA1c means you have too much sugar in your blood and are more likely to develop diabetes complications.

nary_nodes.label: Health insurance coverage for diabetes tests
evidence: The glucose tolerance and the HbA1c tests are not covered by health insurance in Germany and Austria, only the fasting blood sugar one is covered, and that may be influencing the options for people in those countries.

nary_nodes.label: Experts agree on early intervention for T2D
evidence: Experts who spoke to DW agreed that to bring type 2 diabetes numbers down among young people, it's important to know when their blood values get close to the line for the disease, a condition known as being "pre-diabetic."

nary_nodes.label: Lifestyle changes stop diabetes progression
evidence: With lifestyle and nutrition changes, diabetes progression can be stopped in some cases, saving them from a host of health problems later on, which may require regular medication and lead to a reduced life expectancy.
